analysis.title: October employment preview: bouncing back a bit
key_insights: CACIB forecasts October headline NFP at +65k, between +29k in September and +133k in August. Consensus has since risen to +65k as well, with submitted forecasts ranging from +26k to +125k and a Bloomberg whisper number of +70k.

If the forecast is met, the three-month moving average of NFP rises to +76k from +51k, pending revisions. CACIB calls this solid given a sharp drop in the breakeven rate from immigration policy shifts.
CACIB estimates breakeven job growth has fallen from more than +200k per month late in the Biden presidency to possibly below +50k now. The Dallas Fed estimates a value just below 0k.

CACIB expects the unemployment rate unchanged at 4.2%, slightly above the July/August trough and below the 4.5% peak of last November, which CACIB sees as the cycle peak. The Sahm rule threshold is nowhere close to being breached.
The September rise in unemployment came from a rebound in participation, which went from 61.4% in July (61.8% in May) back to 61.8%. CACIB does not read it as labour market weakness.

CACIB expects average hourly earnings of +0.3% MoM in October versus +0.1% in September, with the YoY rate falling to 2.9% from 3.0% on base effects. Soft wage growth supports the Fed's view that labour is not a major inflation source.

October data so far has been mostly solid. ADP rose +86k, both ISM employment components beat expectations and are in expansion, and the Conference Board labour differential is at its highest since April. October NFP has also tended to surprise to the upside historically.

The print is a wild card because of NSA seasonal composition. Education, both private and state and local government, plays a large role, and local government education moved -52k in July and +49k in August on an SA basis.
CACIB describes the labour market as low-hire, low-fire, with demand and supply cooling together and the vacancy-to-unemployment ratio near 1x.

CACIB expects the Fed to hike another 25bp in December. The Fed held in October, helped by larger-than-expected downward revisions to historical PCE data, but September inflation data was less friendly.
CACIB argues next week's October CPI and PPI will likely matter more for the December FOMC than this week's jobs report. An in-line jobs report would leave the focus on inflation.

risk_factors: Local government education hiring has been highly volatile and could swing the October headline number.
Seasonal NSA composition, especially education, makes the October print a wild card.
Next week's October CPI and PPI could change the Fed's December path more than the jobs data.
geopolitical: Restrictive US immigration policy is expected to stay in place for the coming years, keeping labour supply growth and the breakeven payroll pace low.
